newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan smelters' 1996/97 first-half profits seen up.
newsitem.headline: Japan smelters' 1996/97 first-half profits seen up.

text.p: Japan's major non-ferrous metal smelters are poised to report a healthy rise in earnings for the fiscal half-year that ended on September 30, having reaped the benefits of a weaker yen and higher treatment charges, analysts said.

They added that the results would probably be in line with forecasts the companies issued in late May, as the negative impact of the summer's slump in metal prices was largely offset by a greater-than-expected slide in the yen against the dollar.
"The weaker yen is really their lifeboat right now," said Mark Berman, an analyst at Jardine Fleming.
Takuji Takemura, an analyst at Nomura Research Institute, agreed.
"This term there was quite a benefit from the yen's decline," he said.

Japan's six leading non-ferrous metal refining companies, excluding unlisted Nippon Mining and Metals Co, forecast parent current profits in the first half totalling 20 billion yen, well ahead of last year's pace which saw combined current profits of 31.7 billion yen for the entire year.
The six firms, scheduled to announce half-year results in the latter half of this week, forecast the following parent current profits:
Mitsui Mining and Smelting 2.7 billion yen
Mitsubishi Materials Corp 5.0 billion yen
Sumitomo Metal Mining Co 6.0 billion
Dowa Mining Co 3.0 billion yen
Furukawa Co 2.1 billion yen
Toho Zinc Co 1.2 billion yen

The forecasts reflect a continued recovery in profitability at Japan's smelters after spring 1995's surge in the yen -- to a post-World War Two record of 79.75 yen to the dollar -- devastated their bottom lines.
The treatment and refining charges smelters receive from mining companies are denominated in dollars.
Analysts said the smelting companies based their earnings forecasts for the first half on assumptions that the yen would average 100 or 105 to the dollar, although the actual figure was about 108.
Also lifting the smelters' profits in the first half was a rise in treatment and refining charges, analysts said.
High global copper prices in recent years encouraged miners to expand output or develop new mines, leading to a plentiful supply of ore relative to global smelting capacity.
This enabled custom smelting companies like Japan's to demand higher treatment charges, which analysts estimate rose by 15 percent to 25 percent this year.
The smelters' contracts with the miners, however, also include so-called price participation bonuses that boost the smelters' income when copper prices are high.
Japan's smelters lost these bonuses when prices plunged in May and June of this year to 80 cents a pound, their lowest in 2-1/2 years.

"Clearly, price participation bonuses are likely to have disappeared this year," said Hiroyuki Asakawa, vice president of Goldman Sachs Japan. "Their dollar-based revenue (in the first half) will be flat."
Prices of nickel and zinc also fell during the summer, although not as drastically as copper. These two metals also make up a much smaller portion of the smelters' revenue than copper does.
